claim: Dental caries is one of the most prevalent chronic diseases, affecting a significant portion of the global population.
source: Dental caries, commonly known as tooth decay, remains one of the most prevalent chronic diseases, affecting a significant portion of the global population (Peres et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peres et al., 2019

claim: Dental caries results from the complex interplay between bacterial biofilms, dietary sugars, and host factors, leading to the demineralization of tooth enamel and dentin.
source: This condition results from the complex interplay between bacterial biofilms, dietary sugars, and host factors, leading to the demineralization of tooth enamel and dentin (Bowen et al., 2018; Mosaddad et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bowen et al., 2018 and Mosaddad et al., 2019

claim: DPSCs have the ability to differentiate into dentin-forming odontoblast-like cells.
source: In recent years, there has been growing interest in the role of dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) in regenerative dentistry due to their ability to differentiate into dentin-forming odontoblast-like cells and their potential in tooth repair and regeneration (Potdar and Jethmalani, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Potdar and Jethmalani, 2015

claim: The regeneration of the dental-pulp complex is closely associated with inflammation.
source: It is widely recognized that the regeneration of the dental-pulp complex is closely associated with inflammation, especially since dental caries and the subsequent regenerative processes take place within an inflammatory environment (Galler et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Galler et al., 2021

claim: Inflammation serves as a vital biological response for ensuring host survival in the face of infection and tissue injury.
source: Inflammation serves as a vital biological response for ensuring host survival in the face of infection and tissue injury, playing a crucial role in maintaining normal tissue homeostasis (Peiseler and Kubes, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peiseler and Kubes, 2018

claim: The regeneration of the injured tooth is closely tied to inflammation.
source: It is generally accepted that the regeneration of the injured tooth is closely tied to inflammation (Lin and Rosenberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lin and Rosenberg, 2011

claim: Inflammation plays a pivotal role in the regeneration of injured dental tissues by stimulating the recruitment, proliferation, and differentiation of pulp progenitor cells and odontoblasts.
source: Specifically, it plays a pivotal role in the regeneration of injured dental tissues by stimulating the recruitment, proliferation, and differentiation of pulp progenitor cells and odontoblasts (Nakashima et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakashima et al., 2013

claim: The BDNF-TrkB pathway is involved in the survival, development, and function of neurons.
source: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and its receptor, tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), constitute a critical signaling pathway involved in the survival, development, and function of neurons (Ferrer et al., 1999; Huang and Reichardt, 2003; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferrer et al., 1999; Huang and Reichardt, 2003; Zhang et al., 2012

claim: The BDNF-TrkB pathway plays a significant role in the inflammatory response and tissue repair processes.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that the BDNF-TrkB pathway also plays a significant role in the inflammatory response and tissue repair processes (Cappoli et al., 2020; Hang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cappoli et al., 2020; Hang et al., 2021

claim: The overexpression of BDNF in DPSCs has been shown to enhance their regenerative capabilities.
source: The overexpression of BDNF in DPSCs has been shown to enhance their regenerative capabilities, which may be particularly beneficial in the context of dental caries where inflammation and tissue damage are prominent.
evidence: Statement of established finding without specific citation in this sentence

claim: BDNF/TrkB plays a critical role in DPSC odontoblastic differentiation under inflammation.
source: Indeed, our previous study demonstrated the critical role of BDNF/TrkB in the DPSC odontoblastic differentiation under inflammation (Kim et al., 2025).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2025

claim: TNFα-stimulated BDNF/TrkB showed an enhanced odontoblast differentiation of DPSCs.
source: Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα)-stimulated BDNF/TrkB showed an enhanced odontoblast differentiation of DPSCs.
evidence: Statement of prior finding from the authors' previous work

claim: Recombinant BDNF protein has an extremely short half-life, which greatly diminishes its effectiveness.
source: One significant obstacle is the clinical application of BDNF itself as the recombinant protein has an extremely short half-life, which greatly diminishes its effectiveness (Miranda-Lourenço et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Miranda-Lourenço et al., 2020

claim: TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs rapidly increase during odontogenic differentiation.
source: Our data show that TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs rapidly increase during odontogenic differentiation, further amplified by inflammatory inducers and mediators such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), lymphotoxin-alpha, and lipopolysaccharide.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Inflammatory inducers and mediators such as TNFα, lymphotoxin-alpha, and lipopolysaccharide amplify TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs during odontogenic differentiation.
source: Our data show that TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs rapidly increase during odontogenic differentiation, further amplified by inflammatory inducers and mediators such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), lymphotoxin-alpha, and lipopolysaccharide.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Transplantation of CRISPR-engineered DPSCs overexpressing BDNF into inflamed pulp tissue significantly enhanced dentin regeneration in injured teeth.
source: An in vivo dentin formation assessment was conducted using a mouse pulp-capping/caries model, where Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats-engineered DPSCs overexpressing BDNF were transplanted into inflamed pulp tissue. This transplantation significantly enhanced dentin regeneration in injured teeth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in vivo mouse model

claim: Transcriptomic profiling of TNFα-treated DPSCs with and without TrkB antagonist cyclotraxin-B revealed significant changes in gene expression related to immune response, cytokine signaling, and extracellular matrix interactions.
source: To further explore potential downstream pathways, we conducted transcriptomic profiling of TNFα-treated DPSCs, both with and without TrkB antagonist cyclotraxin-B. The results revealed significant changes in gene expression related to immune response, cytokine signaling, and extracellular matrix interactions.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript

claim: Human DPSCs were isolated from third molars of adult donors aged 29–30 years old collected during the extraction of wisdom teeth.
source: Commercially available human DPSCs isolated from third molars of adult donors (ages 29–30 years old) collected during the extraction of wisdom teeth, which were guaranteed and authenticated through 10 population doublings, to express CD105, CD166, CD29, CD90, and CD73, and do not express CD34, CD45, and CD133 106-108
evidence: Description of cell source in methods section

claim: The DPSCs used express CD105, CD166, CD29, CD90, and CD73.
source: Commercially available human DPSCs isolated from third molars of adult donors (ages 29–30 years old) collected during the extraction of wisdom teeth, which were guaranteed and authenticated through 10 population doublings, to express CD105, CD166, CD29, CD90, and CD73, and do not express CD34, CD45, and CD133 106-108
evidence: Description of cell characterization in methods section

claim: The DPSCs used do not express CD34, CD45, and CD133.
source: Commercially available human DPSCs isolated from third molars of adult donors (ages 29–30 years old) collected during the extraction of wisdom teeth, which were guaranteed and authenticated through 10 population doublings, to express CD105, CD166, CD29, CD90, and CD73, and do not express CD34, CD45, and CD133 106-108
evidence: Description of cell characterization in methods section

claim: TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs were significantly upregulated during odontogenic differentiation under inflammatory stimulants such as TNFα, LTA, and LPS by 301±17, 320±15.2, and 250±19, respectively, vs. control 165±12.4 (p<0.01).
source: TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs were significantly upregulated during odontogenic differentiation, especially under inflammatory stimulants such as TNFα, LTA, and LPS by 301±17, 320±15.2, and 250±19, respectively, vs. control 165±12.4 (p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: LPS, LTA, TNFα, and C5a significantly increased TrkB expression in dentinogenic media compared to regular media (p<0.001 for LPS, TNFα, and C5a; p<0.05 for LTA).
source: However, LPS, LTA, TNFα, and C5a significantly increased TrkB expression in dentinogenic media compared to regular media (p<0.001 for LPS, TNFα, and C5a; p<0.05 for LTA).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2

claim: TNFα stimulation caused significant phosphorylation of TrkB (p<0.01) compared to TrkB (p<0.05).
source: TNFα stimulation caused significant phosphorylation of TrkB (p<0.01) compared to TrkB (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by in cell western assay data shown in Figure 2B and D

claim: TrkB expression showed a pronounced peak at 10 ng/mL TNFα in dentinogenic media (p<0.001) compared to 0.1 and 1 ng/mL.
source: The dose-dependent response of TrkB to TNFα (Figure 2E) revealed minimal baseline expression at 0 ng/mL TNFα, with significant increases at 0.1 ng/mL, 1 ng/mL, and a pronounced peak at 10 ng/mL in dentinogenic media (p<0.001) compared to 0.1 and 1 ng/mL.
evidence: Supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2E

claim: TrkB expression in dentinogenic media peaked on day 7 (p<0.001) in response to 10 ng/mL TNFα.
source: The time-dependent response to a fixed TNFα concentration (10 ng/mL) showed that TrkB expression in dentinogenic media was significantly higher on day 1, further increased by day 3, and peaked on day 7 (p<0.001) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by time-course data shown in Figure 2F

claim: STRO-1 was primarily localized around blood vessels in human teeth.
source: The in vivo analysis revealed that STRO-1 was primarily localized around blood vessels, while TrkB was more abundantly expressed in the inflamed pulp tissue of carious teeth compared to normal teeth.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from human tooth sections shown in Figure 3

claim: TrkB was more abundantly expressed in the inflamed pulp tissue of carious teeth compared to normal teeth.
source: The in vivo analysis revealed that STRO-1 was primarily localized around blood vessels, while TrkB was more abundantly expressed in the inflamed pulp tissue of carious teeth compared to normal teeth.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from human tooth sections shown in Figure 3

claim: TrkB expression was significantly elevated in TNFα-treated DPSCs (p<0.01).
source: In vitro, both STRO-1 and TrkB were expressed in control DPSCs, but TNFα treatment markedly increased TrkB expression (Figure 3L–T). The data showed that TrkB expression was significantly elevated in TNFα-treated DPSCs (p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data from cultured DPSCs shown in Figure 3

claim: Transfection of DPSCs with the BDNF CRISPR activation plasmid increased BDNF expression compared to the control group.
source: Transfection of DPSCs with the BDNF CRISPR activation plasmid was confirmed through western blot analysis, which revealed increased BDNF expression compared to the control group (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The dentin volume in the group treated with CRISPR-engineered BDNF-overexpressing DPSCs was 1315±42 mg HA/ccm, significantly higher than the control group which was measured at 1127±20.4 mg HA/ccm (p<0.05).
source: Specifically, the dentin volume in the treated group (Figure 5C) was 1315±42 mg HA/ccm, significantly higher than the control group (Figure 5B), which was measured at 1127±20.4 mg HA/ccm (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT quantification data shown in Figure 5

claim: The BDNF-DPSC transplantation group demonstrated significant tooth regeneration and repair compared to the control group.
source: In contrast to the control group, the BDNF-DPSC transplantation group demonstrated significant tooth regeneration and repair. The newly formed dentin at the injury site appears more organized and closely resembles the native dentin structure.
evidence: Supported by H&E staining analysis shown in Figures 4D and 5

claim: GFP expression was observed in areas correlating with the injury compared to the control.
source: Specifically, GFP expression was observed in areas correlating with the injury compared to the control (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A

claim: DPSCs overexpressing BDNF, engineered using CRISPR and transplanted into a pulp-capping mouse model, significantly improve dentin regeneration.
source: These results indicate that DPSCs overexpressing BDNF, engineered using CRISPR and transplanted into a pulp-capping mouse model, significantly improve dentin regeneration.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results including micro-CT, H&E staining, and immunohistochemistry

claim: The gene heatmap and transcripts heatmap revealed distinct high and low gene expression patterns between the control and TNFα+CTX-B groups.
source: The gene heatmap and transcripts heatmap revealed distinct high and low gene expression patterns between the control and TNFα+CTX-B groups (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing heatmap data shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: The GO enrichment pathway analysis revealed that the highest p-values were associated with the extracellular space and region.
source: The GO enrichment pathway analysis revealed that the highest p-values were associated with the extracellular space and region (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8A

claim: Reactome pathway analysis indicated high p-values for pathways related to TNF signaling.
source: Furthermore, Reactome pathway analysis indicated high p-values for pathways related to TNF signaling (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by Reactome pathway analysis shown in Figure 8B

claim: The transcriptional response of TNFα+CTX-B-treated odontoblast-like differentiated DPSCs showed significant downregulation in TCFs and ATF4 and upregulation in signal transducers and activators of STAT1 and STAT3 compared to the TNFα alone-treated group.
source: The transcriptional response of TNFα+CTX-B-treated odontoblast-like differentiated DPSCs showed significant downregulation in TCFs and ATF4 and upregulation in signal transducers and activators of STAT1 and STAT3 (Figure 8C1) compared to the TNFα alone-treated group (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by transcription factor analysis shown in Figure 8C and C1

claim: TNFα and LTA mediate inflammatory responses and contribute to the recruitment and activation of immune cells at the injury site.
source: TNFα and LTA are known to mediate inflammatory responses and contribute to the recruitment and activation of immune cells at the injury site (Farges et al., 2015; Kawai and Akira, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Farges et al., 2015 and Kawai and Akira, 2010

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines promote the differentiation and activity of odontoblast-like cells, which are responsible for producing the reparative dentin matrix.
source: In the context of dentin formation, these cytokines promote the differentiation and activity of odontoblast-like cells, which are responsible for producing the reparative dentin matrix. (Durand et al., 2006; Keller et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Durand et al., 2006 and Keller et al., 2010

claim: LPS stimulates an inflammatory response when it infiltrates the dental pulp.
source: LPS, components of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, also stimulate an inflammatory response when they infiltrate the dental pulp (Brodzikowska et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brodzikowska et al., 2022

claim: The presence of LPS triggers the release of various pro-inflammatory cytokines, further enhancing the recruitment of immune cells and promoting the processes necessary for tertiary dentin formation.
source: The presence of LPS triggers the release of various pro-inflammatory cytokines, further enhancing the recruitment of immune cells and promoting the processes necessary for tertiary dentin formation (Widbiller et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Widbiller et al., 2018

claim: TNFα can enhance TrkB expression and activation in various cell types, promoting cellular responses to inflammation.
source: These findings are consistent with previous studies indicating that TNFα can enhance TrkB expression and activation in various cell types, promoting cellular responses to inflammation (Irfan et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023b; Paula-Silva et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Irfan et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023b; Paula-Silva et al., 2009

claim: TNFα induced the highest TrkB upregulation in both media types, emphasizing the role of TrkB in mediating responses to neurotrophic factors and involvement in inflammatory pathways.
source: Particularly, TNFα induced the highest TrkB upregulation in both media types, emphasizing the role of TrkB in mediating responses to neurotrophic factors and involvement in inflammatory pathways (Irfan et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Irfan et al., 2022a and experimental data

claim: The differential expression of TrkB in dentinogenic media indicates enhanced receptor sensitivity and signaling in an inflammatory environment.
source: The differential expression in dentinogenic media indicates enhanced receptor sensitivity and signaling in an inflammatory environment (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016 and experimental observations

claim: BDNF-TrkB signaling could be crucial in the neurogenic and angiogenic processes involved in pulp tissue repair.
source: This suggests that BDNF-TrkB signaling could be crucial in the neurogenic and angiogenic processes involved in pulp tissue repair (Bar et al., 2021; de Moraes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bar et al., 2021 and de Moraes et al., 2018

claim: BDNF is known for its role in molecular and physiological involvement.
source: BDNF is known for its role in molecular and physiological involvement (Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2014

claim: BDNF may play a crucial role in odontogenesis and dentinogenesis.
source: Its application in dental tissue engineering suggests it may also play a crucial role in odontogenesis and dentinogenesis (Kim et al., 2023b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2023b

claim: BDNF can enhance the regenerative capabilities of DPSCs, leading to improved outcomes in dentin repair.
source: The significant increase in dentin volume in the micro-CT experiment observed in this study supports the hypothesis that BDNF can enhance the regenerative capabilities of DPSCs, leading to improved outcomes in dentin repair.
evidence: Inference drawn from experimental micro-CT data

claim: BDNF enhances dentin regeneration and creates a conducive environment for tissue repair.
source: This suggests that BDNF enhances dentin regeneration, creating a conducive environment for tissue repair.
evidence: Inference drawn from histological analysis

claim: BDNF may enhance the proliferation and differentiation of DPSCs into odontoblast-like cells, promoting reparative dentin formation.
source: Several potential mechanisms could explain that BDNF may enhance the proliferation and differentiation of DPSCs into odontoblast-like cells, promoting reparative dentin formation (Tsutsui, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsutsui, 2020

claim: The neurotrophic properties of BDNF could support the survival and function of sensory nerve fibers within the pulp, which may play a role in regulating the repair process.
source: Moreover, the neurotrophic properties of BDNF could support the survival and function of sensory nerve fibers within the pulp, which may play a role in regulating the repair process (Bathina and Das, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bathina and Das, 2015

claim: Inflammation enhances the neurogenic potential of DPSCs through TrkB signaling.
source: This suggests that inflammation enhances the neurogenic potential of DPSCs through TrkB signaling.
evidence: Inference drawn from in vitro experimental results

claim: Modulating the inflammatory environment to enhance TrkB signaling could improve the regenerative properties of DPSCs.
source: Modulating the inflammatory environment to enhance TrkB signaling could improve the regenerative properties of DPSCs, offering promising strategies for managing dental caries and pulpitis.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications

claim: TNFα treatment mediated by the BDNF/TrkB pathway induces a complex network of transcriptional changes that modulate the extracellular matrix and inflammatory signaling pathways.
source: These findings suggest that TNFα treatment mediated by the BDNF/TrkB pathway induces a complex network of transcriptional changes that modulate the extracellular matrix and inflammatory signaling pathways (Figure 9).
evidence: Inference drawn from RNA sequencing and pathway analysis data

claim: Several transcriptional factors are involved in BDNF/TrkB downstream signaling, especially the TCF family.
source: We believe that several transcriptional factors are involved in BDNF/TrkB downstream signaling, especially the TCF family.
evidence: Inference from transcriptomic data showing TCF downregulation with TrkB antagonist

claim: The use of CRISPR-engineered BDNF-overexpressing DPSCs could offer a novel and effective approach for enhancing dentin repair and regeneration in cases of dental pulp injury.
source: The use of CRISPR-engineered BDNF-overexpressing DPSCs could offer a novel and effective approach for enhancing dentin repair and regeneration in cases of dental pulp injury and significant clinical implications for dental regenerative therapies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental results and potential clinical implications

claim: This approach could potentially reduce the need for more invasive treatments, such as root canal therapy, and improve outcomes for patients with dental trauma or disease.
source: This approach could potentially reduce the need for more invasive treatments, such as root canal therapy, and improve outcomes for patients with dental trauma or disease.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential clinical applications

claim: Odontoblastic differentiation of DPSCs in response to caries injury takes place within an inflammatory environment.
source: Odontoblastic differentiation of DPSCs in response to caries injury takes place within an inflammatory environment (Chmilewsky et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chmilewsky et al., 2016

claim: TrkB is activated during the caries process.
source: Our findings demonstrate the activation of TrkB during the caries process.

source: Consistent with this, our in vitro data confirmed that various inflammatory mediators increase TrkB expression and activation in DPSCs.

source: These findings suggest that BDNF/TrkB directly affects the pulpal response to caries.

source: In vivo, TrkB is more highly expressed in inflamed pulp compared to normal tissue.

source: The transplantation of CRISPR-engineered BDNF-overexpressing DPSCs in a pulp-capping mouse model significantly enhances dentin regeneration and repair, as demonstrated by increased dentin volume and improved tissue morphology.

claim: RNA sequencing reveals significant transcriptomic changes in TNFα-treated DPSCs, affecting cellular signaling and extracellular matrix pathways.
source: Furthermore, RNA sequencing reveals significant transcriptomic changes in TNFα-treated DPSCs, affecting cellular signaling and extracellular matrix pathways.
evidence: Summary of RNA sequencing results

claim: TrkB plays a critical role in inflammatory responses and dentin repair.
source: These results underscore the critical role of TrkB in inflammatory responses and dentin repair, suggesting potential for targeted TrkB modulation in dental tissue regeneration.

claim: Targeted TrkB modulation has potential in dental tissue regeneration.
source: These results underscore the critical role of TrkB in inflammatory responses and dentin repair, suggesting potential for targeted TrkB modulation in dental tissue regeneration.
evidence: Speculative statement about therapeutic potential

claim: A minimum of 7 days of differentiation is necessary for culturing DPSCs in inflammatory responses related to TrkB expression.
source: The time-dependent response to a fixed TNFα concentration showed a peak at day 7, indicating that a minimum of 7 days of differentiation is necessary for culturing DPSCs in inflammatory responses related to TrkB expression.
evidence: Inference drawn from time-course experimental data

claim: Higher doses of TNFα beyond 10 ng/mL are unnecessary to avoid inflammation related to degeneration or infection.
source: A dose-dependent increase in TrkB expression was observed with escalating TNFα concentrations, with significant upregulation at 10 ng/mL, beyond which further increases in TNFα did not enhance expression. This suggests that higher doses are unnecessary to avoid inflammation related to degeneration or infection (Kim et al., 2023b).
evidence: Inference drawn from dose-response data and citation
